analogy.p: Think of every whole number as a model built from a set of **LEGO bricks**, where the only bricks you are allowed are the prime ones (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ...). The unique factorisation theorem says each model has exactly one recipe of bricks (360 uses three 2-bricks, two 3-bricks and one 5-brick). The **HCF** is the biggest chunk of bricks that both models contain (the bricks they share), while the **LCM** is the smallest set of bricks from which you could build either model (the highest number of each colour you ever need). The analogy breaks down because real bricks can be taken apart in different ways to make different things, whereas a number's prime recipe is fixed, and a LEGO model does not have a 'size' that multiplies the way the numbers do.

bullets: **Know the vocabulary exactly**: factor (divisor), multiple, prime, composite, prime factor, common factor, common multiple, HCF, LCM, coprime, product, index form.
**Write any number as a product of prime factors**, usually in **index form**, e.g. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
**Find the HCF and LCM** of two (or three) numbers using lists, prime factor trees and Venn diagrams.
Use **product notation**: writing a number as 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 or with indices.
Understand the **unique factorisation theorem**: every integer greater than 1 is either prime or can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way (ignoring the order).
Solve **context problems** (buses, lights flashing, tiling, cutting lengths, sharing) by deciding whether the question needs the HCF or the LCM.
Command words are usually **write, express, find, work out, show that** and **write down**; always show the method, because method marks are available even if the final answer slips.
core.p: This point (Edexcel N4) asks you to use the **concepts and vocabulary** of prime numbers, factors (divisors), multiples, common factors, common multiples, **highest common factor (HCF)** and **lowest common multiple (LCM)**, and to use **prime factorisation**, including **product notation** and the **unique factorisation theorem**. On the Higher tier these ideas are the foundation for simplifying fractions and surds, adding fractions, algebraic factorising, ratio, and 'when will two events happen together' problems, so they are tested in short 1 and 2 mark questions and also hidden inside longer problem-solving questions. Both Paper 1 (non-calculator) and Papers 2 and 3 can test them, but the non-calculator paper is where you must do it all by hand.

bullets: Every number has **1** and **itself** as factors, so the smallest list of factors has two entries (for a prime number) except 1 itself, which only has the single factor 1.
**Method for all factors of 36**: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, 6 × 6. List: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36 (nine factors; 6 is only written once).
**Stop at the square root**: for 50, √50 is just over 7, so test 1 to 7: 1 × 50, 2 × 25, 5 × 10. List: 1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50.
The factors of a number are **never bigger than the number**, and a factor is always a whole number (2.5 is not a factor of 10 in this topic).
**Square numbers have an odd number of factors** because one pair is the same number twice (6 × 6). Every other number has an even number of factors.
A factor of a number is also a factor of every **multiple** of that number, e.g. 3 is a factor of 12, so 3 is also a factor of 24, 36 and 120.
**Exam tip**: if the question says 'list all the factors', write them in increasing order and count the pairs; examiners award 2 marks for all correct and 1 mark for at most one error or omission.
core.h: Factors (divisors): definition and how to find them systematically
core.p: A **factor** (also called a **divisor**) of a number is a whole number that divides into it exactly, leaving no remainder. Factors always come in **pairs** that multiply to give the number, so the safest way to find all of them is to test 1, 2, 3, 4, ... in order and write each pair as you find it, stopping when the two sides of the list meet in the middle. You only ever need to test up to the **square root** of the number, because any factor bigger than the square root is paired with one smaller than it. Writing the factors in order and then checking the pairs prevents the most common error, which is missing one out.

bullets: **Factors are small and finite; multiples are large and infinite.** Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, 48, ...
A number is a multiple of n if it can be divided by n with **no remainder**; a quick check is whether it appears in the n times table.
The first multiple of any number is **the number itself** (1 × n), never 0 in GCSE questions unless stated.
**Multiples of 2 are the even numbers**; multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5; multiples of 10 end in 0.
A question like 'write down a multiple of 6 that is between 50 and 60' has the answer **54** (6 × 9); check by dividing 54 ÷ 6 = 9.
'**Write down the first three multiples of 8**' means 8, 16, 24 (not 1, 2, 4 or 0, 8, 16).
Memory trick: **F**actors **F**ew and **F**ound by dividing; **M**ultiples **M**any and **M**ade by multiplying.
core.h: Multiples: definition and how to generate them
core.p: A **multiple** of a number is the result of multiplying that number by a positive whole number; it is what you see in its times table (and continuing past it). The multiples of 7 are 7, 14, 21, 28, 35 and so on forever, so unlike factors there are **infinitely many** multiples. The key relationship is that **factors divide into a number, but multiples are divided by the number**: if 4 is a factor of 12 then 12 is a multiple of 4. Mixing these two words up is the most common vocabulary error in the whole topic, so always attach the correct direction to each.

bullets: **By 2**: the last digit is even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8).
**By 3**: the **digit sum** is a multiple of 3. For 7 413: 7 + 4 + 1 + 3 = 15, which is a multiple of 3, so 7 413 is divisible by 3.
**By 4**: the **last two digits** form a number divisible by 4 (so 3 716 works because 16 ÷ 4 = 4).
**By 5**: the last digit is 0 or 5.   **By 10**: the last digit is 0.
**By 6**: divisible by both 2 **and** 3 (check even, then digit sum).
**By 8**: the **last three digits** form a number divisible by 8 (or halve three times and check each result is a whole number).
**By 9**: the digit sum is a multiple of 9. 5 481: 5 + 4 + 8 + 1 = 18, so divisible by 9.

**By 11**: the **alternating digit sum** (add digits in odd positions, subtract those in even positions) is 0 or a multiple of 11. 2 729: (2 + 2) − (7 + 9) = 4 − 16 = −12, not a multiple of 11, so not divisible by 11. For 918 082: (9 + 8 + 8) − (1 + 0 + 2) = 22, so divisible by 11.
core.p: Divisibility tests let you decide quickly, **without a calculator**, whether a number is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 or 11. They are essential for prime factorisation because you must keep dividing by the smallest prime that works. Most tests work because of the structure of our base-ten place values: for instance 10 is a multiple of 2 and 5, so only the last digit matters for those, while 10 is one more than 9, which is why the digit sum matters for 3 and 9.

bullets: **Common errors**: 1 is not prime; 2 is prime (and the only even one); 9, 15, 21, 27, 33, 39, 51, 57 look prime but are multiples of 3; 49 = 7 × 7 and 91 = 7 × 13 are traps.
**To test whether n is prime**, try dividing by every prime up to √n. For 97, √97 is just under 10, so test 2, 3, 5, 7: none divides, so 97 is prime. For 91: 91 ÷ 7 = 13, so it is composite.
The **Sieve of Eratosthenes** finds primes by crossing out multiples of 2, then 3, 5, 7 and so on; what is left is prime (see the diagram).
There are **infinitely many primes** (proved by Euclid), but there is no simple formula for them; examiners will not ask you to prove this at GCSE.
**Twin primes** are pairs differing by 2 (11 and 13; 17 and 19). Any prime greater than 3 is one more or one less than a multiple of 6.
A number's **prime factors** are the prime numbers that divide into it. The prime factors of 12 are 2 and 3 (not 2, 2, 3 and not 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12).
core.h: Prime numbers, composite numbers and the special case of 1
core.p: A **prime number** is a number with **exactly two factors: 1 and itself**. A number with more than two factors is called **composite**. The number **1 is neither prime nor composite**, because it has only one factor; this is deliberate, and it is exactly what makes the unique factorisation theorem work (if 1 were prime, 6 = 2 × 3 = 1 × 2 × 3 = 1 × 1 × 2 × 3 and the factorisation would not be unique). The only **even prime** is **2**, since every other even number has 2 as a third factor. You are expected to know the primes up to at least 20, and it is very sensible to learn them up to 100.

bullets: **Check your answer by multiplying back**: 2³ × 3² × 5 = 8 × 9 × 5 = 360. This takes ten seconds and catches nearly every slip.

**Product notation** means a product written with × signs, e.g. 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. **Index form** collapses repeated factors: 2² × 3² × 5. Read the question to see which is asked; 'product of prime factors' accepts either, but 'in index form' needs powers.
If a question says 'write 84 as a product of its prime factors', a full-mark answer is **2² × 3 × 7** (4 × 3 × 7 = 84).
**Do not stop early**: 4 × 3 × 7 is not a prime factorisation because 4 is not prime. Every number in the final product must be prime.
Any correct tree order works; if two students draw different trees they must still end with the same primes.
core.h: Prime factorisation: factor trees and repeated division
core.p: Prime factorisation means writing a number as a **product of prime numbers only**. There are two reliable methods. In a **factor tree** you split the number into any two factors, then keep splitting each composite branch until every branch ends in a prime (ring each prime as you reach it). In **repeated (ladder) division** you divide by the smallest prime that goes in, then the next, until you reach 1. Both give the same answer because of the unique factorisation theorem, so you can pick whichever you find easier. Always finish by writing the primes **in ascending order** and converting to **index form**.

bullets: **Unique** means exactly one set of primes with exactly one set of indices; it does not depend on the route you took.
It **needs 1 not to be prime**; otherwise you could add any number of 1s into the product.
**Perfect square test**: a number is a perfect square if **every index in its prime factorisation is even**. 144 = 2⁴ × 3², so 144 = (2² × 3)² = 12².
**Perfect cube test**: every index is a multiple of 3. 216 = 2³ × 3³ = (2 × 3)³ = 6³.
**Square root from the factorisation**: halve each index. √(2⁶ × 5²) = 2³ × 5 = 40.
**Making a square**: to find the smallest number to multiply 72 by to get a square, 72 = 2³ × 3². The index of 2 is odd, so multiply by **2** to get 2⁴ × 3² = 144 = 12².
Any number that is a **multiple of n** must contain, in its prime factorisation, all of the primes of n with at least the same indices.
core.h: The unique factorisation theorem (fundamental theorem of arithmetic)
core.p: The **unique factorisation theorem** states that every integer greater than 1 is either a prime number or can be written as a product of prime numbers, and that this product is **unique apart from the order of the factors**. That is why 360 will always come out as 2³ × 3² × 5 however you split the tree, and why we say 'the' prime factorisation rather than 'a' prime factorisation. This single idea is what lets us compare two numbers prime by prime to find the HCF and LCM, and it also lets us decide things like whether a number is a perfect square or cube without finding its square root.

bullets: A **prime** p = p¹ has (1 + 1) = **2** factors, which agrees with the definition.
A number has an **odd** number of factors only when every (index + 1) is odd, i.e. every index is even, which is the same as being a perfect square.
**To list the factors systematically**, take each prime in turn: for 12 = 2² × 3, the factors are 2⁰,2¹,2² multiplied by 3⁰,3¹: 1, 2, 4, 3, 6, 12.
Any factor of a number uses **only the primes in that number**, with each index no larger than in the number.
Showing the working (a + 1)(b + 1) earns the method mark even if you slip arithmetically.
core.h: Counting factors from the prime factorisation (Higher extension)
core.p: Once a number is written in index form, you can **count its factors without listing them**. If N = p^a × q^b × r^c (with p, q, r different primes), then every factor is built by choosing how many copies of each prime to use: 0 up to a copies of p, 0 up to b copies of q, and 0 up to c of r. The choices are independent, so the number of factors is **(a + 1)(b + 1)(c + 1)**. This is an extension that appears in problem-solving questions on Higher papers, and it is very good for checking a list of factors.

bullets: **Listing method**: factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24; factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, so **HCF = 12**.
**Prime factor method**: 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3². Take the lowest power of each shared prime: 2² and 3¹. HCF = 2² × 3 = **12**.
The HCF is **at most the smallest of the numbers**, and it is exactly that number if it divides the others (HCF of 6 and 18 is 6).
**Coprime** numbers have an HCF of 1 (e.g. 8 and 15); they share no prime factors.
For three numbers, use only primes that appear in **all three**, with the lowest index in any of them.
Every common factor of two numbers is also a factor of their HCF (the common factors of 24 and 36 are the factors of 12).
**Link to fractions**: dividing the top and bottom of 24/36 by their HCF 12 gives 2/3 in one step, which is fully simplified.
**Link to algebra**: taking out the HCF of the numbers in 12x + 18 gives 6(2x + 3).
core.h: Common factors and the highest common factor (HCF)
core.p: A **common factor** of two or more numbers is a number that divides exactly into all of them. The **highest common factor (HCF)** is the largest such number. HCF answers questions where you must **split into equal groups of the biggest possible size**, or **simplify a fraction fully**, so it always involves something getting smaller or being shared out. There are two main methods: list the factors of each number and pick the largest one in both lists, or compare prime factorisations and multiply the primes they **share**, using the **lowest power** of each shared prime.

bullets: **Listing method**: multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 ...; multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24 ... The first match is **12**, so LCM = 12 (the next common multiple, 24, is also a multiple of the LCM).
**Prime factor method**: 12 = 2² × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3². Highest powers: 2² and 3². LCM = 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = **36**.
The LCM is **at least as big as the largest number**, and equals it if the other numbers are factors of it (LCM of 3 and 12 is 12).
For **coprime** numbers the LCM is simply their product (LCM of 8 and 15 is 120).
**Every common multiple is a multiple of the LCM**, so the times when two events coincide are 1 × LCM, 2 × LCM, 3 × LCM, and so on.
**Link to fractions**: the LCM of the denominators is the **lowest common denominator** for adding or subtracting fractions (1/4 + 1/6: LCM of 4 and 6 is 12).
**Link to ratio and rotation problems**: gears with 12 and 18 teeth line up again after 36 teeth have passed.
core.h: Common multiples and the lowest common multiple (LCM)
core.p: A **common multiple** of two or more numbers is a number that appears in all of their multiple lists, and the **lowest common multiple (LCM)** is the smallest one. LCM answers questions about things that **repeat and meet up again**: buses leaving a station, lights flashing, gears turning, or finding a common denominator. The two methods mirror those for HCF: list multiples until the first match, or use the prime factorisations, taking **every prime that appears in either number**, each to its **highest power**.

bullets: **Setting up for 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3**: shared primes are one 2 and one 3, so the overlap holds **2 and 3**; the 12-only region holds **2**; the 18-only region holds **3**.
**HCF** = product of the overlap = 2 × 3 = **6**.
**LCM** = product of everything = 2 × 3 × 2 × 3 = **36**.
**Check using the relationship**: for any two numbers, **HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers**. Here 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18.
If the question gives a half-filled Venn diagram and one of the products, use division to find missing numbers inside it.
A number that is in neither circle but in the universal set (a rectangle) can be included for 'numbers 1 to 20'-style Venn questions about factors and multiples; read the labels carefully.
The relationship HCF × LCM = a × b only works for **two** numbers, not three.
core.h: Venn diagrams for HCF and LCM
core.p: A **Venn diagram** is the neatest way to find the HCF and the LCM together, and it is the method examiners most often ask you to **complete**. Write each number's prime factors in its own circle, but put the primes that **both** numbers share in the **overlap**. Then the **HCF is the product of the numbers in the overlap**, and the **LCM is the product of every number in the whole diagram** (overlap counted once). It works because the overlap holds exactly the lowest powers of the shared primes, and the whole diagram holds the highest powers of every prime.

bullets: **LCM clue words**: 'at the same time again', 'next time together', 'first day both', 'every ... minutes', 'smallest number that both go into'.
**HCF clue words**: 'largest possible', 'greatest size', 'equal groups with none left over', 'cut into pieces of equal length', 'largest square tile'.
**Example (LCM)**: bus A every 12 minutes and bus B every 20 minutes, both leave at 08:00. LCM of 12 and 20 is 60, so they next leave together at **09:00**.
**Example (HCF)**: a 48 cm by 36 cm rectangle is cut into identical squares with no waste; the largest square has side HCF(48, 36) = **12 cm**.
**Sharing**: 40 pens and 56 pencils shared into identical packs with nothing left over; the maximum number of packs is HCF(40, 56) = 8.
**Show the method**: list or write prime factorisations; a bare final answer risks losing all marks if it is wrong.
Give a **final sentence in context** (e.g. 'They next leave together at 09:00').
core.h: Solving context problems: HCF or LCM?
core.p: Word problems are where most marks are lost, usually because students pick the wrong one. The decision rule is simple. If the situation involves **splitting, cutting, sharing or tiling into the largest equal pieces**, the answer is a **factor**, so use the **HCF**. If the situation involves **repeating events that meet again**, or the **first time two patterns line up**, the answer is a **multiple**, so use the **LCM**. After computing, always put the answer back in context, with units or a time, and check that it is sensible.

bullets: **Fractions**: simplify by dividing top and bottom by the HCF; add using the LCM of the denominators.
**Surds**: simplify √72 by writing 72 = 36 × 2 (largest square factor), giving 6√2.
**Algebra**: taking the **highest common factor out** of an expression, e.g. 6x²y + 9xy² = 3xy(2x + 3y).
**Algebraic fractions**: the lowest common denominator is the LCM of the denominators, e.g. LCM of 4x and 6x² is 12x².
**Ratio and proportion**: reducing 48 : 60 to its simplest form by dividing by HCF 12 gives 4 : 5.
**Proof**: 'Show that the sum of three consecutive integers is a multiple of 3' uses the idea of a multiple.
**Index laws**: multiplying prime factorisations adds indices and dividing subtracts them, e.g. (2³ × 3²) × (2 × 3) = 2⁴ × 3³.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam-style connections
core.p: Prime factorisation, HCF and LCM underpin large parts of the Higher course. Spotting them in disguise is what separates grade 6 from grade 9 work. Simplifying fractions, ratios and surds all reduce to cancelling common factors; adding fractions or algebraic fractions needs a lowest common denominator, which is an LCM; and the 'show that' proofs about even, odd and multiples rely on the idea of a factor and unique factorisation.

bullets: Present factor trees with **ringed primes** and write a clear final line such as **'360 = 2³ × 3² × 5'**.
Write the **prime factorisations of both numbers one above the other** before comparing them, lining up the primes.
**Check HCF**: it must divide exactly into every number in the question. **Check LCM**: every number must divide exactly into it.
For large numbers (e.g. 252 and 420), factorise: 252 = 2² × 3² × 7 and 420 = 2² × 3 × 5 × 7; HCF = 2² × 3 × 7 = **84**; LCM = 2² × 3² × 5 × 7 = **1260**.
**Non-calculator safe multiplication**: break into chunks, e.g. 4 × 9 × 35 = 36 × 35 = 1 260.
If the answer is requested **'as a product of prime factors'**, do not multiply it out. If the answer is requested **'as a number'**, multiply it out.
Where a question has a **given Venn diagram**, copy the numbers carefully and do not re-use a prime more times than the numbers allow.
core.h: Calculation skills and presentation for full marks
core.p: Examiners award marks for method as well as accuracy, so the way you set out prime factorisation, HCF and LCM matters. Neat, labelled working also lets you spot errors. Use your own check every time: multiply the primes back, or test that your HCF divides both numbers and that both numbers divide your LCM.

exam: **Command words**: 'write' and 'write down' need no working but 'show that' and 'work out' do; always show factor trees or lists in case of an error.

**1 mark** questions: 'Write down a multiple of 7 between 30 and 40' (35), 'Write down a prime number between 20 and 30' (23 or 29), or 'Is 51 prime?' (No, because 51 = 3 × 17). Always give a reason when the question says 'explain'.
**2 mark** 'list all the factors of 28': 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28 earns both marks; one error or omission scores 1 mark.
**2 to 3 marks** 'Write 540 as a product of its prime factors': method mark for a correct factor tree or division, answer 2² × 3³ × 5 for the final mark. State **index form** if asked.
**Find HCF and LCM** (usually 3 or 4 marks): method mark for prime factorisations of each number, answer marks for HCF and for LCM. Venn diagram questions give marks for correct placement.
**'Show that' questions**: you must show full working that reaches the given answer, ending with a clear conclusion; do not just state it.
**Context problems (3 or 4 marks)**: decide HCF vs LCM, show the calculation, then **answer in context** with units or the time of day.
**Model phrase for primes**: 'A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself.' Use it whenever you are asked to explain why a number is not prime: give a factor other than 1 and the number.
**Calculator papers**: you can use a calculator to check, but the prime factorisation still needs to be shown; a factor-tree button is not enough on its own.
**Check before you leave the question**: multiply back the primes, and test that the HCF divides both numbers and that both numbers divide the LCM.
**Higher tier 6 mark problem-solving**: expect the idea to be combined with another topic such as fractions, ratio or proof, so write each step clearly with a reason.

mistakes.r: 1 is **not prime** because it has only one factor. The first prime is 2.
**2 is prime and even**, and it is the only even prime.
mistakes.w: Saying all prime numbers are odd.

mistakes.r: Every branch must end in a **prime**; keep splitting composite numbers.
mistakes.w: Stopping a factor tree at 4, 6, 9 and so on.

mistakes.r: The **HCF uses the lowest power of the shared primes**; the LCM uses the highest power of all primes.
mistakes.w: Writing the HCF using the highest power of each prime.

mistakes.r: Factors **divide into** the number (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12); multiples are found by **multiplying** it.
mistakes.w: Mixing up factors and multiples, e.g. listing 3, 6, 9 for factors of 12.

mistakes.r: Only coprime numbers have LCM equal to the product. 6 = 2 × 3 and 8 = 2³, so LCM = 2³ × 3 = **24**.
mistakes.w: Giving the LCM of 6 and 8 as 48 (the product).

mistakes.r: Work in **pairs** (1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, 6 × 6) until the pairs meet.
mistakes.w: Missing factor pairs when listing, e.g. the factors of 36 without 9 or 18.

mistakes.r: Write **2² × 3²**. Read whether the question asks for index form or just a product.
mistakes.w: Giving an answer such as 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 and being asked for index form.

mistakes.r: Events that repeat and meet again need the **LCM**; sharing or cutting into equal biggest pieces needs the **HCF**.
mistakes.w: Choosing HCF for a 'when do the buses meet again' problem.

summary: You need to use the vocabulary of factors, multiples, primes, common factors, common multiples, HCF and LCM, write numbers as products of prime factors (including index form and the unique factorisation theorem), and apply these to problems. It matters because the same ideas drive simplifying fractions and surds, adding fractions, algebraic factorising and 'next time together' problems.

terms.d: A whole number that divides exactly into another number with no remainder.
The result of multiplying a number by a positive whole number; a number in that number's times table.
A number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself. The first prime is 2.
A whole number greater than 1 that has more than two factors, i.e. is not prime.
A factor of a number that is itself a prime number.
Writing a number as a product of prime numbers only.
The result of multiplying numbers together.
A way of writing repeated multiplication using powers, e.g. 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 2² × 3³.
A number that is a factor of two or more given numbers.
The largest number that divides exactly into two or more given numbers.
A number that is a multiple of two or more given numbers.
The smallest positive number that is a multiple of two or more given numbers.
Two numbers whose only common factor is 1, i.e. HCF = 1.
Every integer greater than 1 is prime or can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order.
A number that is the square of an integer; all indices in its prime factorisation are even.
A quick rule using the digits of a number to decide whether it is divisible by another number without dividing.

worked.q: (a) Write 360 as a product of its prime factors, in index form. [3 marks] (b) How many factors does 360 have? [2 marks]
steps: Collect the primes: 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5, then use indices: 2³ × 3² × 5.
(b) The indices are 3, 2 and 1, so number of factors = (3 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.

worked.q: Find (a) the HCF and (b) the LCM of 84 and 90. [4 marks]
steps: HCF uses the shared primes with the lowest powers: 2¹ and 3¹, so HCF = 2 × 3 = 6.
LCM uses every prime with its highest power: 2², 3², 5 and 7, so LCM = 4 × 9 × 5 × 7 = 36 × 35 = 1 260.

worked.q: Two lighthouses flash at 08:00. Lighthouse A flashes every 12 seconds and lighthouse B every 20 seconds. (a) After how many seconds do they next flash together? (b) A rectangular sheet 48 cm by 36 cm is cut into identical squares with no waste. What is the side of the largest possible square? [4 marks]
steps: (a) Events that repeat and meet again, so use the LCM. 12 = 2² × 3 and 20 = 2² × 5, so LCM = 2² × 3 × 5 = 60.
They flash together again after 60 seconds.
(b) Largest equal pieces, so use the HCF. 48 = 2⁴ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3².
HCF = 2² × 3 = 12, so the side of the square is 12 cm (4 squares by 3 squares).
Check: 48 ÷ 12 = 4 and 36 ÷ 12 = 3, both whole numbers, and 12 is the largest such number.
